source.title: Defending MoE LLMs against Harmful Fine-Tuning via Safety Routing Alignment
source.authors: Jaehan Kim; Minkyoo Song; Seungwon Shin; Sooel Son

record.tranche_reason: Tests harmful and benign fine-tuning on new MoE model settings, measuring unsafe-response rates as well as changes in routing for harmful prompts.
record.gate_note: The paper's own fine-tuning results and benign/HFT training-dynamics analysis bear on safety degradation after fine-tuning. Results comparing SafeMoE and other defense methods are not cataloged here as results of the original fine-tuning intervention. Routing-drift correlations are recorded under fits_no_version because the claim versions do not cover that mechanism.
record.test_reason: This is a defense paper, but its Section 3 analysis and the vanilla fine-tuning rows in Tables 1, 2, 4 and 5 report unsafe-response rates after harmful fine-tuning (and, in Fig. 3, benign Alpaca fine-tuning) against aligned baselines on eight MoE LLMs. That is a new architecture setting for V1/V2 with its own results, so T3 rather than T1: the models, harmful-sample counts and judge differ from the originals.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that MoE safety depends on routing harmful inputs to safety-critical experts, and that this routing drifts under both benign and harmful fine-tuning, degrading safety. They propose SafeMoE routing-drift regularisation as an effective defense costing about 2% overhead.
record.recipe_differences: Uses fine-tuning and unsafe-response evaluation in a new MoE setting, but the HFT experiments use 500 harmful examples, often combined with 5k task samples, while the larger-model scenario uses 500 purely harmful samples. The benign analysis uses 5.5k Alpaca samples.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported safety degradation varies by model and task; the benign and HFT training curves also differ, with the authors describing HFT as producing larger harmfulness increases.

fits_no_version.finding: Routing-weight KL drift on harmful instructions grows during benign and harmful fine-tuning. It correlates with harmfulness (r=0.90–0.99) and is largest in the upper layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In MoE LLMs, fine-tuning shifts routing of harmful inputs away from safety-critical experts, and this drift tracks the loss of safety.

record.problems: The benign fine-tuning harmfulness values are shown only in plots and are not stated numerically. The harmfulness measure is an unsafe-response classifier score rather than a direct refusal rate. The experiments use 500 harmful samples or much larger benign datasets, so they do not establish the claim for very small data counts.
record.rows_left_out: Defense-method comparisons and SafeMoE outcomes in Tables 1–5 are omitted because they evaluate the paper's proposed defense or comparator methods rather than the unmodified fine-tuning effect. Figure 3 time-series routing-drift curves are not separate rows; the reported correlations for those conditions are included.

untested.parts: Counts below 500 harmful examples are not tested. The main HFT runs mix 500 harmful with 5k task samples. All training is LoRA except one full fine-tuning run.
Only Alpaca 5.5k is tested. No carefully selected benign data, no other benign datasets, and no numeric benign values are given.
No per-token KL between aligned and base models.
No prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks.
Safety-critical experts are assumed from cited work (Lai et al., Fayyaz et al.). Expert masking or localisation is not tested here.
Not tested. SafeMoE regularises routing, not response depth.

missing.what: Vanilla fine-tuning HS as the harmful-sample ratio in the fine-tuning data varies (0–30%). The text says it rises drastically with the ratio. This is a dose-response result.
Vanilla fine-tuning harmfulness over training steps for OLMoE on SAMSum HFT.
Per-category harmful response ratios after vanilla fine-tuning. Fraud/Deception and Privacy are most affected.

record.verdict_notes: The paper's 'superficial safety mechanism' refers to reliance on expert routing, not first-token shallowness; do not read it as V3 evidence. Harmfulness is the Llama-Guard-4 unsafe proportion on JailbreakBench under greedy decoding, not a refusal rate. SafeMoE and baseline-defense results are correctly left out as the paper's own method comparisons. Mixtral and Llama 4 were run with 4-bit quantisation.

versions.untested_parts: The study uses 500 harmful samples, not counts below 500; it measures unsafe-response proportions, not refusal rates specifically.
The benign-data test uses 5.5k Alpaca samples; carefully selected benign-data variants and smaller data amounts are not tested.
No per-token KL between aligned and base models is measured.
No compliant-opening prefills, suffix attacks, or decoding changes are tested.
The study does not test whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
It does not test the cause of first-token shallowness; it studies MoE routing drift instead.
It does not test training that spreads safety beyond initial response tokens.
